 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping First Reviews: A Familiar but Thrilling Return to Form
 Critics say the latest chapter of Panem history follows a similar path as its predecessors, but fans will appreciate the briskly paced, action-packed journey.
 By
 Christopher Campbell 
 | Published November 17, 2026 
 TAGGED AS: Action , movies 
 Panem returns to the big screen this week with the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping , and the first reviews of the prequel are now online. Based on the dystopian novel of the same name, this sixth movie in the franchise depicts the 50th Hunger Games and features a teenage Haymitch (played by a well-cast Joseph Zada ) among the tributes. The ensemble also includes Mckenna Grace , Elle Fanning , Ralph Fiennes , Kieran Culkin , and Jesse Plemons , most as younger versions of characters we know and love. The result is said to be better than the last movie, but perhaps a bit too overstuffed with familiar roles and story beats.

 Directed By:

 Here’s what critics are saying about The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping :
 Is it a worthy addition to the franchise? 
 Director Francis Lawrence delivers a brutal, beautifully crafted, and emotionally devastating return to The Hunger Games universe that reminded me exactly why I fell in love with this franchise in the first place.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 This is a pulse-pounding, heartbreaking, and thrilling epic; a rousing and brilliant addition to the saga that continues to set the bar for the genre.
– Joonaten Itkonen, Region Free 
 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has flashes of dark, fascinating brilliance.
– Justin Clark, Slant Magazine 
 It digs into the same ideas of submission, rebellion, and loss that power the series at its best.
– Matt Oakes, Silver Screen Riot 
 Familiar formula and all, this is the closest I’ve come to loving one of these movies again.
– Manuel São Bento, Movies We Texted About 
 Sunrise on the Reaping feels like a return to form, but some aspects of that original form didn’t work, and this movie has all those warts as well.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 Sunrise on the Reaping is a good, entertaining movie… But the movie is good in spite of the nostalgia-based, franchise-minded storytelling that constantly threatens to smother it.
– Alex Harrison, Screen Rant 
 The film functions more as an exercise in how younger actors would take on supporting characters from the original quartet of movies. Some do it better than others, but it’s all more of a curiosity than a reason to play the games again.
– Matt Goldberg, Commentary Track 
 (Photo by ©Lionsgate) 
 How does it compare to the other Hunger Games movies? 
 Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes , to the spirit of the first movies.
– David Rooney, The Hollywood Reporter 
 Unlike The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , it’s been directed, by Francis Lawrence, in that lavish mode of surface intensity we might now call Hunger Games Classic.
– Owen Gleiberman, Variety 
 As a character study, it also works much better on Haymitch than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes did on Snow.
– Manuel São Bento, Movies We Texted About 
 This is the most depressing Hunger Games film by far (bring all the tissues).
– Lauren LaMagna, Next Best Picture 
 Tonally and emotionally, the film is lighter, despite much of what happens being presented as profoundly tragic.
– Alex Harrison, Screen Rant 
 While it mirrors the first prequel in clunky structure and pacing, the ending, in particular, somehow manages to drag the whole thing down in a really unfortunate way.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 It’s the first entry in the series since 2013’s Catching Fire to feel as if it’s mostly covering well-trodden territory.
– Justin Clark, Slant Magazine 
 Do you need to be a longtime fan of the franchise to enjoy it? 
 A moving coda set many years later reintroduces familiar faces that will add to the satisfaction for longtime franchise fans.
– David Rooney, The Hollywood Reporter 
 Lawrence is giving fans of these films exactly what they’re looking for here, and as someone who’s enjoyed them, it works.
– Alex Harrison, Screen Rant 
 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will make a lot of fans happy at the end of the day; for everyone else, it’s about as good as The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , for good and for ill.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 While this movie is part of a series, it could easily be a standalone film with an interesting yet heartbreaking plot…[It] could be enjoyed by almost any audience member.
– Allison Rose, FlickDirect 
 Even the staunchest fans may feel the same about this trip back in time to the 50th Hunger Games, since in most respects it’s akin to a greatest-hits package.
– Nick Schager, The Daily Beast 
 (Photo by Murray Close/©Lionsgate) 
 How does it compare to the book? 
 Lawrence does an excellent job of trying to keep as much of the source material intact.
– Allison Rose, FlickDirect 
 Trying to stuff most of Collins’ tome into 158 minutes, Lawrence’s film shortchanges everything.
– Nick Schager, The Daily Beast 
 The structure and pacing of a book don’t always translate to a movie, and in this case, Sunrise on the Reaping stumbles.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 How does it look? 
 This movie has the same overall look and feel as the others, as Lawrence tends to fluctuate between wide establishing shots and close-ups to build tension. He also uses a variety of colors that pop off the screen to grab the audience’s attention.
– Allison Rose, FlickDirect 
 Sunrise on the Reaping looks vastly different from both the original saga and The Battle of Songbirds and Snakes … The film has a psychedelic quality that emphasizes the colors purple, green, and yellow.
– Lauren LaMagna, Next Best Picture 
 The cinematography, costumes, set design, and visual effects create a version of Panem that feels both familiar and newly realized.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 Imagine the first two Hunger Games films had been made in the 1970s by Nicolas Roeg… The production design and cinematography evoke a certain morose ’70s kitsch.
– Justin Clark, Slant Magazine 
 At first, this arena’s vibrant colors and CGI forest critters give everything a deeply artificial sheen that reeks of CGI. Then you realize the artificiality is the point.
– Matt Goldberg, Commentary Track 
 Despite opulent sets and extravagant outfits, Sunrise on the Reaping is visually flat, not least because we’ve seen similar Panem sights countless times before.
– Nick Schager, The Daily Beast 
 (Photo by Murray Close/©Lionsgate) 
 Are the games thrilling? 
 This is the first time the Games actually feel like a proper event… The action is also clearly improved.
– Manuel São Bento, Movies We Texted About 
 The nail-biting Arena action is vicious and bloody.
– David Rooney, The Hollywood Reporter 
 The deaths we see this time around might be the most brutal ones in the series so far.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 The action might be familiar, and familiarly brutal, but it is no less spectacular.
– Joonaten Itkonen, Region Free 
 The spectacle never completely overwhelms the tragedy. The action is impressive, but the emotional consequences are what give it meaning.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 There is a substantial lack of action and violence…The lack of 87Eleven, the original stunt team, is not only missed but immensely felt.
– Lauren LaMagna, Next Best Picture 
 Does it overstay its welcome? 
 This latest installment is just over two and a half hours long, but it doesn’t drag or feel too long at any point.
– Allison Rose, FlickDirect 
 Unlike some lengthy blockbusters that leave you checking your watch, I found the experience completely worthwhile.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 At two hours and forty minutes, Sunrise on the Reaping moves like a freight train: slow at first, then picking up speed so fast the final act trips over itself as it ties everything together.
– Joonaten Itkonen, Region Free 
 (Photo by ©Lionsgate) 
 How is Joseph Zada as young Haymitch? 
 Any reason this movie works is because of Joseph Zada.
– Kaitlyn Booth, Bleeding Cool 
 Joseph Zada is a legitimately excellent find…He carries the film with a depth and intensity that even Jennifer Lawrence sometimes struggled to summon while leading the franchise.
– Matt Oakes, Silver Screen Riot 
 The surprise asset here is Australian actor Joseph Zada in a breakout performance.
– David Rooney, The Hollywood Reporter 
 It was a role he was truly born to play; a true star-is-born moment in a star-is-born role.
– Lauren LaMagna, Next Best Picture 
 It is a brilliant performance; magnetic and charming.
– Joonaten Itkonen, Region Free 
 What impressed me most was how naturally Zada bridges the younger character with the Haymitch audiences recognize.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 Like a taller version of Christopher Atkins in The Blue Lagoon …he’s the young warrior as pin-up.
– Owen Gleiberman, Variety 
 What about the rest of the younger cast? 
 Jesse Plemons, playing a role originated on screen by Philip Seymour Hoffman, is the clear standout.
– Alex Harrison, Screen Rant 
 The Oscar-nominated Plemons at least strikes a resonant chord as Plutarch.
– Nick Schager, The Daily Beast 
 Ralph Fiennes brings an amoral coldness to President Snow that feels much more of a piece with Tom Blyth’s teenage take on the character in Ballad .
– Justin Clark, Slant Magazine 
 Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket almost steals the film…Fanning lights up the screen with a performance that unifies the character across the decades and actors in a single shot.
– Joonaten Itkonen, Region Free 
 Kieran Culkin is another standout as Caesar Flickerman. He is excellent.
– Nagier Chambers, Big Gold Belt Media 
 Culkin is fine, but not nearly as stylishly depraved as Stanley Tucci.
– Owen Gleiberman, Variety 
 Kieran Culkin as young Caesar Flickerman…gives a performance so bad it makes you wonder if we’ve misjudged his ability this whole time.
– Matt Goldberg, Commentary Track 
 (Photo by ©Lionsgate) 
 What is the movie’s biggest fault? 
 A big part of the folly of the Hunger Games prequels is that they’re about the “evolution” of a dystopia…that’s already a dystopia! (How much of a thrill is it to see things slide from bad to a little bit worse?)
– Owen Gleiberman, Variety 
 There are too many legacy characters and actors that demand screen time.
– Lauren LaMagna, Next Best Picture 
 Lawrence wrongly assumes he doesn’t need to develop these figures because they’ve already been established, and the result is that they all resonate as two-dimensional shadows of their former (older) selves.
– Nick Schager, The Daily Beast 
 My one disappointment is the Quarter Quell twist itself. Twice as many tributes is a nice idea that the film barely uses, as the vast majority are dispatched off-screen so quickly that it might as well be the usual 24.
– Manuel São Bento, Movies We Texted About 
 Every time the movie lurches into high-camp excess, it lessens the emotional weight.
– David Rooney, The Hollywood Reporter 
 The Hunger Games has lost its ability to be harrowing. For a series about children fighting to the death, that isn’t a great sign.
– Alex Harrison, Screen Rant
